question: NPC: What happens between writing and running
intro: I'm Nia, the Logic-Weaver. The code you write is not what the machine runs. This scene is about what happens in between.

steps.say: Your **source code** is never run as it stands. The **compiler**, `javac`, reads `BankAccount.java` and translates it into **bytecode**, which it stores in `BankAccount.class`. Bytecode is not the language of any one computer. It is written for the **Java Virtual Machine**, the JVM: a program that every kind of computer has its own copy of.

beats.say: Your **source code** is never run as it stands. The **compiler**, `javac`, reads `BankAccount.java` and translates it into **bytecode**, which it stores in `BankAccount.class`.

beats.code:
javac BankAccount.java
    → makes BankAccount.class
java BankAccount
    → the JVM loads and runs it

beats.say: Bytecode is not the language of any one computer. It is written for the **Java Virtual Machine**, the JVM: a program that every kind of computer has its own copy of.

check.prompt: Which file does the JVM load and run?
check.why: The `.java` file is for people and for the compiler. What the JVM loads is the bytecode in the `.class` file, and the same `.class` file runs on any system that has a JVM.

steps.say: While this runs, the JVM keeps its data in separate areas of memory. The call gets a **frame** on the **stack**, holding its parameters and local variables: `rate`, and `acct`. The object that `new` makes lives on the **heap**. `acct` holds only a **reference** to it. When openAccount returns, its frame is removed at once, and `rate` and `acct` go with it.

check.prompt: openAccount returns, and its frame is removed. What happens to the BankAccount object?
check.answer: It stays on the heap until the garbage collector removes it
wrong: It is removed along with the frame, at once
check.why: Objects are never kept in a frame, so they do not go with one. Once nothing refers to an object, the **garbage collector** is free to remove it from the heap.

steps.say: A mistake can show up at two moments. `javac` checks the text, and a **compile error** stops it there: no `.class` file is made, so there is nothing to run. Other mistakes depend on values that exist only while the program runs. Java reports those by throwing an **exception**, and exceptions are the second half of this chapter.

outro: First, the journey from source to running program. Then, what Java does when a running program goes wrong.

question: Arrange what happens to a Java class, from the moment you write it to the moment it runs.
items: You write BankAccount.java, the source code
javac compiles the source into bytecode
The bytecode is stored in BankAccount.class
The JVM's class loader brings the class into memory
The JVM's execution engine runs the bytecode
feedback: Source code is for people. javac translates it once into bytecode, kept in a .class file. Nothing runs yet: running is the JVM's job. When the program is started, the JVM loads each class as it is needed and its execution engine carries out the bytecode.

question: What does a .class file hold?
correct: Bytecode: instructions written for the Java Virtual Machine
incorrect: Machine code for the one computer on which it was compiled
The source code again, with its comments and spaces removed
A saved copy of every object the program made as it ran
feedback: javac does not produce the machine code of any particular computer. It produces bytecode, a lower-level form of your program that the JVM knows how to carry out. The source is not in there, and neither are objects, which only exist while a program runs.

question: The same compiled banking program runs on a Windows desktop, a Mac laptop and a Linux server, without being compiled again. Why?
correct: Each system has its own JVM, and every JVM runs the same bytecode
incorrect: javac writes a separate machine-code file for each kind of system
The source code travels along, and is compiled again on arrival
All three systems use the same processor instructions underneath
feedback: Bytecode is written for the JVM, not for Windows or for a particular processor. Each system has a JVM built for it, and that JVM stands between the bytecode and the machine. So one .class file serves everywhere a JVM exists.

question: Match each part of the Java Virtual Machine to its job.

pairs.definition: Finds a .class file and brings it into memory when it is first needed
Holds every object the program makes
Holds a frame for each method call, with its local variables
Holds what belongs to a class as a whole, such as static variables
Removes objects that nothing refers to any more
Turns bytecode that runs often into fast machine code

feedback: The class loader brings classes in as they are needed. Memory is divided by purpose: objects on the heap, method calls and local variables on the stack, class-level information in the method area. The garbage collector clears the heap of objects no longer referred to, and the just-in-time compiler speeds up the bytecode that is used most.

question: A banking program has hundreds of classes. When does the JVM load VillainAccount.class into memory?
correct: The first time the running program needs VillainAccount
incorrect: At the start, along with every other class of the program
While javac is compiling, before the program is ever run
Each time an object is made with new VillainAccount(…)
feedback: Classes are loaded when they are first needed and not before, which lets a large program start quickly. A class the run never touches is never loaded. Once loaded, a class stays: making a second VillainAccount does not load it again.

question: The class loader meets a class for the first time. Arrange the three things it does, in order.
items: Loading: the .class file is found and its bytecode is read into memory
Linking: the bytecode is verified, and its references to other classes resolved
Initialization: the static initialization code of the class is run
feedback: Load, link, initialize. The bytecode has to be in memory before it can be checked, and it has to be checked and connected to the classes it mentions before any of its code is allowed to run. Initialization is where static variables get their starting values.

correct: count and the reference gru on the stack; the object on the heap
incorrect: count on the stack; the reference gru and the object in the method area
count, the reference gru and the object all together on the stack
count on the heap; the reference gru and the object on the stack
feedback: Local variables live in their method's frame on the stack, and gru is a local variable: it holds a reference. The BankAccount object that the reference leads to was made with new, and every object lives on the heap. The method area holds class-level information, not objects and not local variables.

question: deposit() has a local variable, fee. What happens to fee when a call of deposit() finishes?
correct: Its stack frame is removed at once, and fee goes with it
incorrect: It waits on the heap until the garbage collector removes it
It moves to the method area, ready for the next call to use
It keeps its value, and the next call of deposit() begins there
feedback: Each call of a method gets its own frame on the stack for its parameters and local variables, and the frame is removed the moment the call ends. Nothing has to clean it up, which is why the stack is fast. The garbage collector works on the heap, where objects are; and a later call gets a fresh frame with a fresh fee.

correct: Each call waits on another call, until the call stack has no room left
incorrect: The int result climbs past Integer.MAX_VALUE, which overflows the stack
The calls create too many objects, so the heap has no memory left
The method loops forever, and Java halts any loop that runs too long
feedback: count has no base case, so every call makes another call before it can return. Each unfinished call occupies a frame on the call stack, and the stack is finite. An int that overflows just wraps around silently, no objects are created here, and Java never stops a loop for running long. StackOverflowError is an Error rather than an Exception: fix the recursion, do not catch it.

question: class Bank has  static int totalAccounts  and  String branchLocation.  A program makes 50 Bank objects. How many of each variable are there?
correct: One totalAccounts, shared by all; fifty branchLocations, one each
incorrect: Fifty totalAccounts and fifty branchLocations: one each per object
One totalAccounts and one branchLocation: all fifty share both
Fifty totalAccounts, one each; one branchLocation, shared by all
feedback: A static variable belongs to the class itself. It exists once, in the method area, however many objects are made, or even if none are. An instance variable belongs to each object: every Bank on the heap has its own branchLocation.

question: One of these counters is static. What does the program print?
feedback: localAccounts is an instance variable, so north and south each have their own: north opened two accounts and south one. totalAccounts is static, so there is only one of it, shared; all three calls of open() added to the same counter.

question: Bank has  public static String getBankName()  and  public String getBranchInfo().  Which line compiles in a main method that has made no Bank object?
correct: String s = Bank.getBankName();
incorrect: String s = Bank.getBranchInfo();
String s = this.getBankName();
String s = getBranchInfo();
feedback: A static method belongs to the class and is called through the class name, with no object needed. getBranchInfo() is an instance method: it reports on one particular branch, so it needs a Bank object in front of the dot. And main is itself static, so there is no this in it.

question: Which of these mistakes does the compiler catch, before the program ever runs?
correct: A semicolon missing from the end of a statement
A String stored in a variable declared as double
deposit("fifty dollars") where deposit takes a double
A private field read from outside its own class
incorrect: An int divided by a variable that turns out to hold 0
A method called on a variable that turns out to be null
A withdraw method that adds where it should subtract
feedback: javac checks what it can see in the text: the syntax, the types of values and arguments, and who may reach what. It cannot know what a variable will hold when the program runs, so a zero divisor and a null show up only then, as exceptions. And a method that does the wrong sum is a logic error: it compiles, it runs, and it is wrong.

question: A bank program accepts withdraw(-50) and the balance goes UP by 50. No error message appears anywhere. What kind of error is this?
correct: A logic error: the program runs, but does the wrong thing
incorrect: A syntax error: the compiler ought to have rejected it
An exception: Java throws one when a result is wrong
A type error: a negative number is the wrong type here
feedback: Nothing is wrong with the grammar or the types, so it compiles; and no rule of Java is broken as it runs, so nothing is thrown. Java has no idea that a negative withdrawal makes no sense to a bank. Only the programmer can prevent it: by testing the amount, and throwing an exception when it is not acceptable.

correct: Java creates an exception object and throws it, ending the program
incorrect: The array quietly grows to six slots so that the write can succeed
The write is skipped and the program carries on at the next line
The value is stored in the nearest valid slot, which here is a[2]
feedback: Index 5 does not exist in a 3-slot array, and Java never resizes an array, skips the line or guesses another slot. Instead it builds an object describing the problem (here an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException) and throws it. A thrown exception that nothing catches ends the program with a stack trace. The rest of this set is about catching it instead.

question: Each snippet compiles but fails when it runs. Match each snippet to the exception it throws.
feedback: The name of an exception tells you what went wrong: a method called on null, text that is not a number, an array index outside 0..length-1 (a[2] is one past the end of a 2-slot array), a cast to a type the object is not, integer division by zero, and a list asked for a position it does not have.

question: Which of these statements about Java's family of exception classes are true?
correct: Throwable is at the top, above both Error and Exception
RuntimeException is one of the subclasses of Exception
NullPointerException is a subclass of RuntimeException
incorrect: Error is the subclass of Exception for the serious cases
IOException is one of the subclasses of RuntimeException
Exception is a subclass of RuntimeException, not above it
feedback: Throwable is the root. Under it are two branches, Error and Exception, side by side. Under Exception, one subclass is special: RuntimeException, the parent of the unchecked exceptions such as NullPointerException. The other subclasses of Exception, IOException among them, are the checked ones.

question: A program uses up all its memory, and Java throws an OutOfMemoryError. How should ordinary banking code treat an Error like this one?
correct: Leave it alone: an Error is a system problem beyond the program's control
incorrect: Catch it as it would any exception, and move on to the next transaction
Declare it with throws, because every Error is a checked exception
Put each use of new inside a try, since any object could be one too many
feedback: The Error branch is for serious trouble in the system itself, such as running out of memory. A program can rarely do anything sensible about it, so application code does not try to catch Errors. What it catches are Exceptions: problems it can foresee and respond to.

question:
A program crashes and prints this stack trace:

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero
    at Shop.share(Shop.java:{{t}})
    at Shop.report(Shop.java:{{m}})
    at Shop.main(Shop.java:{{b}})

On which line number of Shop.java was the exception actually thrown?
feedback_template: Read a stack trace from the top. The first "at" line is where the exception was thrown: inside share, on line {{expected}}. Each line below it is a caller that was still waiting: report called share from line {{m}}, and main called report from line {{b}}. Start debugging at the top line that is in your own code.

question: NPC: The line that never runs
intro: An exception does not have to end a program. You can put the risky lines inside a `try`, and say in a `catch` what to do if one of them throws.

steps.say: A **try block** says: attempt these lines. The **catch block** after it says: if an exception of this type is thrown in there, run these lines instead. Trace it like the machine. The first line of the `try` prints `start`. Nothing has gone wrong yet.

beats.say: A **try block** says: attempt these lines. The **catch block** after it says: if an exception of this type is thrown in there, run these lines instead.
Trace it like the machine. The first line of the `try` prints `start`. Nothing has gone wrong yet.

steps.say: parseInt cannot read `"7x"`, so it **throws** a NumberFormatException. The instant an exception is thrown, Java abandons the rest of the try block and jumps to the catch whose type matches.

beats.say: parseInt cannot read `"7x"`, so it **throws** a NumberFormatException. The instant an exception is thrown, Java abandons the rest of the try block and jumps to the catch whose type matches.

check.why: It sits after the line that threw, inside the try. Java never comes back to finish a try block.

steps.say: The catch prints `oops`. The exception is now **handled**, so the program carries on below the try statement. Had nothing been thrown, the catch would have been skipped instead: `start`, `parsed`, `after`.

beats.say: The catch prints `oops`. The exception is now **handled**, so the program carries on below the try statement.

figure.alt: Flow: print start, then parseInt of 7x, which throws. The thrown route goes to the catch, which prints oops, and on to print after. The other route, through print parsed, is dimmed.
figure.caption: The dim route is the one taken when nothing is thrown.

beats.say: Had nothing been thrown, the catch would have been skipped instead: `start`, `parsed`, `after`.

outro: The next monster throws a different exception. Find the line that never runs.

question: Trace this code. What does it print?
correct:
A
null!
ok
feedback: A prints normally. s.length() is a method call on null, so it throws a NullPointerException: that println never gets a value to print, and B is skipped because Java abandons the rest of the try block. The matching catch prints null!, the exception is now handled, and execution continues after the try statement with ok.

feedback_template: "{{a}}" and "{{b}}" parse, so they are added. "x" and "{{c}}y" are not whole numbers, so parseInt throws before += can happen and the catch subtracts 1 instead, twice. Because the try sits inside the loop, each failure is handled and the loop moves on to the next word. Total: {{expected}}.

question: Here the whole loop is inside the try. What does the code print?
correct:
3
bad
end
feedback: "3" parses and prints. "x" throws, and the jump to the catch leaves the try block, which means it leaves the loop too, so "5" is never reached. Java does not go back into a try block after the catch finishes. To keep looping past a bad item, the try has to be inside the loop body.

answer.expr: min(n, m) + min(1, max(0, m - n))

feedback_template: The array has {{n}} slots, indexes 0 to {{last}}, and the loop asks for i from 0 up to one less than {{m}}. Every pass with a valid index prints one line. If i ever reaches {{n}}, the assignment a[i] = i throws before that pass can print; the catch then prints stop once and the loop is over for good. If i never reaches {{n}}, nothing is thrown and the catch is skipped. Total lines here: {{expected}}.

question: The method throws an exception with a message, and the caller catches it. What does this print?
correct:
40
short
feedback: The first call passes its test and prints 40. In the second, amount is more than balance, so the method makes an exception object carrying a message and throws it: its own println never runs, and neither does the third call, which is abandoned with the rest of the try. The catch receives the object as e, and e.getMessage() hands back the text it was made with.

question: Three catch blocks follow one try. What does the code print?
correct:
R
end
feedback: Casting a String to Integer throws a ClassCastException, so A is skipped. Java tries the catch blocks from the top and runs the FIRST one whose type fits. ClassCastException is not a NullPointerException, but it is a subclass of RuntimeException, so R prints. Only one catch ever runs: the Exception block would also fit, but Java has stopped looking.

question: One try, three catch blocks, four calls. What does the program print?
correct:
ok
N
P
big
feedback: Each call can fail in a different place, and each failure has its own catch. "lots" is not a number, so parseDouble throws a NumberFormatException: N. A null account has no length() to call, a NullPointerException: P. And 999 is over the limit, so the code throws an IllegalArgumentException itself, and the last catch prints its message. Only one catch runs per call, the first whose type fits.

correct: It does not compile: the second catch is unreachable
incorrect: It compiles, and the first catch handles the exception
It compiles, and the more specific second catch handles it
It compiles, and both catch blocks run, one after the other
feedback: Catch blocks are tried top to bottom and the first fit wins. Every NumberFormatException is also an Exception, so the first block would take them all and the second could never run. Java treats that as a mistake and refuses to compile: "exception NumberFormatException has already been caught". Put subclasses above their superclasses.

question: FileNotFoundException extends IOException, and IOException extends Exception. One try block is followed by these three catch blocks. Arrange them from top to bottom so that the code compiles.
feedback: Most specific first. A catch for a superclass also takes all of its subclasses, so any subclass block placed below it could never run, and Java rejects that as a compile error. Going from FileNotFoundException to IOException to Exception, each block gets first pick of its own cases before a broader one sees them.

question: A try block holds three statements, and the second one throws an exception that the catch block matches. The try statement also has a finally block. Arrange what happens, from first to last.
items: The first statement in the try block runs
The second statement throws, so the third is skipped
The statement after the whole try statement runs
feedback: A throw abandons the rest of the try block, the matching catch handles the exception, and then the finally block runs. finally runs on every way out of a try, which is why cleanup goes there. Only after finally does execution continue below the try statement.

question: What does this code print?
correct:
A
C
F
end
feedback: A prints, then 10 / 0 throws an ArithmeticException, so B is skipped. The matching catch prints C, the finally block prints F, and the program continues with end. Remove the division and the output would be A, B, F, end: the catch is skipped when nothing is thrown, but finally still runs.

question: The finally block runs whichever way the try goes. What does this print?
correct:
UIL
UBL
feedback: U is for unlock, I for in, B for bad code, L for lock. With "12345" nothing is thrown: the try runs to its end, the catch is skipped, and finally adds L. With "abc" parseInt throws, so I is skipped and the catch adds B; then finally adds L just the same. Whatever happened in between, the vault ends up locked.

correct: A and F, then a NullPointerException stack trace
incorrect: A, C, F and end, because the catch block handles the failure
A, F and end, because the finally block clears the exception
A, then a NullPointerException stack trace straight away
feedback: A catch only handles the type it names (or a subclass of it), and a NullPointerException is not an ArithmeticException, so C never prints. The finally block still runs on the way out, printing F, but finally does not handle anything: the exception keeps going, end is never printed, and with no other handler the program stops with a stack trace.

question: This try block returns. What does the code print?
correct:
T
F
1
feedback: return 1 works out the value to hand back, but before the method is allowed to leave, its finally block runs and prints F. Only then does the caller receive 1 and print it. Not even a return gets past a finally block, which is what makes it a safe home for cleanup code.

question: new FileReader("accounts.txt") can throw FileNotFoundException, which is a checked exception. What does "checked" mean for code that makes a FileReader?
correct: It will not compile unless that line is caught or declared
incorrect: It is detected at compile time, so it cannot happen at run time
It must be caught in the same method; it cannot be passed on
It is more serious, so the program halts even when it is caught
feedback: "Checked" means checked by the compiler: it insists that the calling code either catches the exception or declares it with throws and passes it on. The failure itself still happens at run time (the file really may be missing), and checked says nothing about severity. Unchecked exceptions, which are RuntimeException and its subclasses, get no such compile-time check.

question: NPC: The compiler demands a plan
intro: Here is a four-line method. This one never even gets to run: the compiler refuses it.

steps.say: `new FileReader(…)` opens a file for reading. Its header in the Java library ends with `throws FileNotFoundException`: a warning that the file might not be there. So `javac` refuses to compile `load`: FileNotFoundException is a **checked exception**. Checked means the compiler checks that you have a plan for it. There are exactly two plans.

beats.say: `new FileReader(…)` opens a file for reading. Its header in the Java library ends with `throws FileNotFoundException`: a warning that the file might not be there.
So `javac` refuses to compile `load`:

beats.code:
error: unreported exception
FileNotFoundException; must be caught
or declared to be thrown

beats.say: FileNotFoundException is a **checked exception**. Checked means the compiler checks that you have a plan for it. There are exactly two plans.

steps.say: Plan one: **catch** the FileNotFoundException right here, and decide what `load` should do when the file is missing. Plan two: **declare** it. Add `throws FileNotFoundException` to the method's **header**, its first line, and the exception is allowed to pass through.

beats.say: Plan one: **catch** the FileNotFoundException right here, and decide what `load` should do when the file is missing.
Plan two: **declare** it. Add `throws FileNotFoundException` to the method's **header**, its first line, and the exception is allowed to pass through.

check.prompt: With plan two, `load()` compiles. Who has to deal with FileNotFoundException now?
wrong: The FileReader class handles it itself
check.why: `throws` does not handle anything. It moves the same catch-or-declare duty up to the caller.

steps.say: Whether an exception is checked depends on its place in the family tree of exception classes. RuntimeException and every class below it are **unchecked**: the compiler asks for no plan. For a checked one, choose the plan that fits: catch where you can do something useful, declare where your caller is better placed to decide.

beats.say: Whether an exception is checked depends on its place in the family tree of exception classes. RuntimeException and every class below it are **unchecked**: the compiler asks for no plan.

figure.alt: A class tree. Exception is at the top, marked checked. Below it, IOException, marked checked, with FileNotFoundException, checked, below that. Also below Exception, RuntimeException, marked unchecked, with ArithmeticException, unchecked, below it.
figure.caption: Below RuntimeException, nothing is checked.

beats.say: For a checked one, choose the plan that fits: catch where you can do something useful, declare where your caller is better placed to decide.

outro: The next monster has the same compile error from a different method. Pick every repair that works.

correct: Add throws InterruptedException to the method header
Wrap the call in a try with catch (InterruptedException e)
Wrap the call in a try with catch (Exception e)
incorrect: Wrap the call in a try with catch (RuntimeException e)
Wrap the call in a try that has only a finally block
Add throw InterruptedException to the method header
feedback: A checked exception must be caught or declared. Declaring uses throws (with an s) in the header. Catching works with the exact type or any superclass, so catch (Exception e) satisfies the compiler too, though it is broader than good style wants. RuntimeException is not a superclass of InterruptedException, so that catch does not cover it; a finally block runs cleanup but catches nothing; and throw (no s) is a statement, not part of a header.

correct: Jam
Clog
incorrect: Leak
Drip
Rust
feedback: What decides it is the family tree. Anything with RuntimeException among its ancestors is unchecked: Leak directly, Drip through Leak, and Rust through IllegalArgumentException, which itself extends RuntimeException. Jam extends Exception without passing through RuntimeException, so it is checked, and Clog inherits that. (Error and its subclasses, such as StackOverflowError, are unchecked as well.) NullPointerException also extends Exception, but so does IOException: it is RuntimeException in the ancestry that makes the difference.

question: NPC: An exception climbs the call stack
intro: An exception that a method does not catch does not vanish. It climbs, up to that method's caller.

steps.say: `a` calls `b`, and `b` calls `c`. While `c` runs, the other two are paused, each waiting for its call to return. That chain of waiting calls is the **call stack**. `c` divides by zero, so an ArithmeticException is thrown. `c` has no try around that line, so `c` ends on the spot and `c done` never prints.

beats.say: `a` calls `b`, and `b` calls `c`. While `c` runs, the other two are paused, each waiting for its call to return. That chain of waiting calls is the **call stack**.

figure.alt: Three boxes in a column: a, waiting for b; below it b, waiting for c; below that c, running and highlighted, at the line 1 / 0. Arrows labelled calls lead from a to b and from b to c.
figure.caption: The call stack while c runs.

beats.say: `c` divides by zero, so an ArithmeticException is thrown. `c` has no try around that line, so `c` ends on the spot and `c done` never prints.

steps.say: The exception now arrives in `b`, at the line that called `c`, exactly as if that line had thrown it. Moving up to the caller like this is called **propagation**.

beats.say: The exception now arrives in `b`, at the line that called `c`, exactly as if that line had thrown it. Moving up to the caller like this is called **propagation**.

check.prompt: `b` has no try/catch either. What happens in `b`?
check.answer: `b` ends at once; `b done` never prints
wrong: `b` prints `b done`, then passes it up
The program crashes, as `b` has no catch
check.why: A method with no matching catch is abandoned just like `c` was, and the exception keeps climbing to its caller.

steps.say: In `a`, the call `b()` sits inside a try with a matching catch, so the climb stops there and `a` prints `a caught it`. Had no method caught it, the exception would have climbed out of `main` too, and the program would end with a **stack trace**: a list of the calls it climbed through.

beats.say: In `a`, the call `b()` sits inside a try with a matching catch, so the climb stops there and `a` prints `a caught it`.

figure.alt: The same three boxes. Arrows labelled ArithmeticException climb from c up to b and from b up to a. c and b are dimmed and marked abandoned; a is marked catch, and prints a caught it.
figure.caption: The exception climbs until a catch fits.

beats.say: Had no method caught it, the exception would have climbed out of `main` too, and the program would end with a **stack trace**: a list of the calls it climbed through.

outro: Now trace one yourself. Watch which lines get abandoned on the way up.

question: inner throws, and the only catch is two calls away. What does the code print?
feedback: inner prints 1, then a[3] throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. inner has no catch, so it is abandoned (no 2) and the exception propagates to outer, which has no catch either (no 3). Back in the try block, the rest is skipped (no 4). ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException is a subclass of RuntimeException, so the catch fits and prints 5, and then the program continues with 6.

correct: The method may let an InsufficientFundsException out to its caller
incorrect: The method throws an InsufficientFundsException each time it is run
The method catches any InsufficientFundsException thrown inside it
The method is where the InsufficientFundsException class is declared
feedback: A throws clause is a warning written into the first line of a method: this exception may come out of here. It does not throw anything (that is the statement throw, with no s), it does not catch anything, and it does not create the class. It tells callers what they have to be ready for.

correct: Error: pay has to catch the exception, or declare it with throws
incorrect: Nothing: pay throws nothing itself, so it has no duty to do anything
A warning only: pay compiles, and may crash later when it is run
Error: a method that throws may be called only from inside main
feedback: A checked exception puts a duty on every caller. pay calls a method that may throw one, so pay has two choices: wrap the call in a try with a catch for it, or add throws InsufficientFundsException to its own first line and pass the duty to whoever calls pay. Doing neither is a compile error, not a warning.

prompt: Fill in the three keywords so that setAge compiles and rejects a negative age.
feedback: throws (with an s) lives in a method header and declares what the method may let escape; it is required here because Exception is checked. throw (no s) is a statement that actually raises one, and what it raises is an object, so it has to be built with new. Everything after a throw that runs is skipped, which is why "age set" is not printed for a negative age.

prompt: Complete this custom checked exception so that getMessage() returns the text handed to its constructor.
feedback: A custom exception is just a class that extends an existing exception type: Exception makes it checked, RuntimeException would make it unchecked. Passing the message up with super(message) lets the inherited getMessage() return it. this(message) would call this same constructor again, which Java rejects.

question: A custom exception in use. What does the code print?
correct:
zap
need 5
feedback: cast(9) passes the test and prints zap. cast(2) throws, so its own println is skipped AND the rest of the try block in the caller is abandoned: cast(7) never happens. The catch prints the message that the constructor passed up with super(m). Because LowMana extends Exception it is checked, which is why cast must say throws LowMana.

question: Which of these is the best case FOR writing a try/catch?
correct: Integer.parseInt on text the user typed, so the program can ask them to try again
incorrect: An array loop that runs one index too far, so the loop can come to a quiet end
A method call on a variable you forgot to initialise, so the run can continue
A division by a counter your own code wrongly left at zero, to skip the sum
feedback: Catch an exception when the cause is outside your control and you have a sensible recovery: users do type nonsense, and asking again is a real fix. The other three are bugs in your own code. Catching them hides the bug and leaves the program running with wrong data; the right repair is to fix the loop bound, initialise the variable, or correct the counter.

question: Which of these claims about handling exceptions well are sound?
correct: An empty catch block hides the failure and makes the bug harder to find
A method that can do nothing useful about an exception may let it propagate
incorrect: Wrapping the whole of main in catch (Exception e) is what makes a program reliable
A NullPointerException caused by your own bug is best dealt with by catching it
Catching ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException is a tidy way to finish an array loop
feedback: Catch the most specific type, and only where you can actually respond; otherwise let it travel to a caller who can. An empty catch throws away the one clue you had. A blanket catch (Exception e) around everything treats a typo-level bug and a missing file the same way and usually just hides both. Bugs such as a null you forgot to set or a loop that overruns should be fixed, not caught: a loop should stop because of its condition.

question: A user types letters where an account number belongs, and the program catches the NumberFormatException. Which message is the most use to that user?
correct: Invalid account number: please use digits only
incorrect: An error has occurred. Please try again later
Exception in thread main: NumberFormatException
Operation failed with code 17: contact the bank
feedback: A good message says what was wrong and what to do about it, in the user's terms. "An error has occurred" says neither. The name of a Java class means nothing to a customer, and a code number sends them off to ask somebody else.

question: A low-level method, validateAccount, finds an account number that does not exist. The screen the user sees is drawn by code three calls above it. Which design follows the lecture's advice?
correct: validateAccount throws; the code that draws the screen catches, and shows a message
incorrect: validateAccount catches the problem itself and prints nothing, so as not to disturb
Each method in between catches the exception, prints it, and throws a new one upward
validateAccount returns as normal, and leaves the screen code to notice it somehow
feedback: Handle an exception where something useful can be done about it. The low-level method is the one that can detect the problem; the user-interface code is the one that can tell the user. Propagation carries the exception from one to the other with no code in between. Swallowing it hides the failure, and catching it at every level only adds noise.

question: Put it all together. What does the code print?
correct:
2
F
F
C
G
feedback: step(5) prints 2 and its finally prints F. In step(0) the division throws before anything is printed; step has a finally but no catch, so F prints on the way out and the exception propagates to the caller. There the rest of the try is abandoned, so step(1) never runs. The catch fits the ArithmeticException and prints C, and the outer finally prints G last.

check.prompt: A row says `throws IllegalArgumentException`. Your method returns -1 for that call. Does the row pass?
check.answer: No: it has to throw, not return
check.why: An exception is not a return value. The row asks for the call to be ended by a throw, and nothing else will do.

It leaves out two things. There is no printStackTrace here, so show an exception's message instead: And it will not run a finally block that returns or throws. Keep `finally` for clean-up.

outro: Short ones, all of them. A `try`, a `catch` or two, sometimes a `finally`. Go.

question: Write parsePrice. It turns text into a price with Double.parseDouble. If the text is not a number, it catches the NumberFormatException and returns -1.0 instead.
hint: One try, one catch. The try holds the return that might fail; the catch holds the return for when it does.
feedback: Double.parseDouble either hands back a number or throws. When it throws, the return in the try never completes, and control jumps to the catch, which returns the fallback value. Every path through the method ends in a return, so Java is satisfied.

question: Write getPotionName. It returns potions[index]. If the index is outside the array, it catches the ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and returns "Unknown".
signature: public String getPotionName(String[] potions, int index)
hint: Let the array decide whether the index is good: read potions[index] inside the try.
feedback: Reading potions[index] with a bad index throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, whether the index is too large or negative, and for an empty array every index is bad. The catch names exactly that exception, and supplies the answer for that case.

question: Write withdraw. If amount is more than balance, it throws  new IllegalArgumentException("Insufficient funds").  Otherwise it returns what is left.
signature: public double withdraw(double balance, double amount)
hint: throw is a statement, and what it throws is an object: throw new IllegalArgumentException("…");
feedback: A method that cannot do what it was asked says so by throwing. throw needs an exception object, made with new and given a message. Nothing after the throw runs, so the return is reached only when the amount was acceptable. IllegalArgumentException is unchecked, which is why the first line needs no throws.

question:
Write processWithdrawal, with two catch blocks.
Parse amountText with Double.parseDouble. If the amount is 0 or less, throw  new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive").
Return  Dispensing $20.0  if all is well;  Error: not a valid number  if it would not parse;  and  Error:  followed by the exception's message  for the other failure.
hint: The catch for NumberFormatException has to come first: every NumberFormatException is also an IllegalArgumentException.
feedback: Two things can go wrong, and each gets its own catch. The order is not free here: NumberFormatException is a subclass of IllegalArgumentException, so a catch for IllegalArgumentException placed first would take both, and Java refuses to compile a catch that can never run. The second catch reads the message from the exception the try itself threw.

question:
Finish access, using finally. It unlocks the vault (locked = false), then returns "Granted" if readCode(code) is 12345 and "Denied" if it is another number.
Do not catch anything: a code that is not a number should still throw. But however access ends, the vault must be locked again.
hint: A try may have a finally and no catch at all. Put  locked = true;  in the finally, and nowhere else.
feedback: There are three ways out of this try: two returns, and the exception that readCode throws for a code that is not a number. A finally block runs on every one of them, so one line there locks the vault whatever happened. Locking it before each return would miss the third way out, and the last test checks exactly that.

question: Write the exception class LoanException. It needs one thing: a public constructor that takes a String message and hands it up to Exception.

tests.run: LoanException e = new LoanException("Amount too small");
Exception e = new LoanException("Score must be 1-10");

hint: The constructor has one line: super(message);
feedback: An exception class of your own is an ordinary subclass. Everything an exception does, it inherits: all this class adds is a constructor, and all the constructor does is pass the message up with super(message), so that the inherited getMessage() can hand it back. Because it extends Exception and not RuntimeException, it is a checked exception.

question: Finish validateLoan. If amount is under 1000 it throws  new LoanException("Amount too small").  If score is not from 1 to 10 it throws  new LoanException("Score must be 1-10").  Otherwise it returns  Gru approved for $5000
signature: public String validateLoan(String name, int amount, int score) throws LoanException
hint: Two ifs, each with a throw inside. The return comes after both, with no else needed.
feedback: LoanException is checked, so a method that throws one and does not catch it has to say so: that is the throws LoanException on the first line, which is given. Each throw ends the method on the spot, so the return is reached only by a loan that passed both tests.

question:
Finish processApplication, with try, catch and finally. It calls validateLoan(name, amount, score), which is given above.
If that returns, the result is what it returned. If it throws, the result is  Denied:  followed by the exception's message. Either way,  (done)  is added on the end:
Gru approved for $5000 (done)
Denied: Amount too small (done)
signature: public String processApplication(String name, int amount, int score)
hint: Declare  String result = "";  before the try, so that the try, the catch and the finally can all use it.
feedback: validateLoan detects the problem and throws; this method, one level up, decides what to say about it. Because it catches the LoanException, its own first line needs no throws. The variable is declared before the try because a variable declared inside a block is gone when the block ends, and the finally adds its part on both paths.
